title: Now she says she can cast out demons
excerpt: Liana Shanti, the spiritual teacher ordered to pay three Canadians $56 million for defamation, has posted her first public exorcism video.
content:
An American alleged cult leader who was ordered to pay three Canadians more than $56 million in a defamation case claims she is an exorcist and that a former supporter’s son will soon be possessed by a demon.

Liana Shanti, whose legal name is Liane Wilson, is an online Hawaii-based spiritual teacher who says she has performed several exorcisms. An exorcism is a religious ceremony that purports to drive out demons from people who are possessed by them.

This week on an online publishing platform, she wrote that she’s performed the controversial religious rites over the past 10 years. She says all of those were done one-on-one and in private.

Until now.

“[T]oday I did something I have never done in my life…I filmed and posted my first ANOINTED DELIVERANCE video on Instagram…an exorcism,” says her post.

In the video she refers to, posted on Tuesday, Liana Shanti isn’t performing a ritual on another person, but is being filmed in a room on her own speaking directly to camera.

“I now revoke every form of access for every demon that tried to enter you through the mRNA technology,” she says in an apparent reference to the COVID-19 vaccine. Shanti has long railed against the vaccines, repeating conspiracy theories that say they are dangerous and calling them part of “Satan’s plan.”

Claims former student is ‘possessed’

Shanti’s recent postings on exorcism take direct aim at a Canadian former-follower.

Amanda Brady from Regina was a student of Liana Shanti for eight years. She now believes she was under the influence of a cult leader and testified against her at her August defamation trial in Honolulu.

Liana Shanti claims to have performed five exorcisms on one of Amanda Brady’s children and now says that the child will be in “FULL DEMONIC POSESSION [sic]” “within three years.”

“I saw the face of the demon in [the child],” says the Instagram post. “The child has no control. This demon is growing stronger. Daily.”

Shanti also writes that “the demon” she refers to “fully occupies Amanda herself.”

In a phone interview with W5, Amanda Brady says the online attacks were expected and she refuses to let them hurt her.

“I really don’t put any weight into what she’s saying because she can be so cruel and she’s so vindictive and all of this is coming from a place of rage and anger,” she says. “She’s not out there right now doing God’s work and anybody who believes that is sorely mistaken.”

Brady adds that she believes Liana Shanti is attacking her to send a message to her current students.

“All of this is to intimidate those who are still there to make sure that they know what’s going to happen to them if they leave,” she says.

“She’s trying to intimidate me. She’s trying to intimidate every other woman from the community who’s watching this from speaking,” she says.

The message from Jesus

In her online blog, Liana Shanti tells the story of performing her very first exorcism – which she also calls a “deliverance” - on an Australian woman 10 years ago. She writes that the woman complained about having nightmares and “weird, negative thoughts.”

“I knew instantly it was a demonic energy,” she writes. “Since the age of two I have been able to see and feel the presence of demons.”

She writes that she was reluctant to perform the exorcism but was convinced by Jesus.

“I kept saying to Jesus… I do not know how. I do not know how to do this. I have never done this. I do not know how. And Jesus said… YOU DO,” she writes.

She says the moment the demon was cast out, the Australian woman told her that a gust of wind blew through her room and knocked over an essential oil diffuser.

Shanti claims the cause of the “demonic possession” was the husband’s pornography habit.

Driving out demons is not the only supernatural power that Liana Shanti claims to have.

In the W5 documentary, Fake Filtered Cult Leader, former students say the spiritual teacher claimed to be psychic and would repeatedly state that followers had been sexually abused as children. She then encouraged them to publicly “out” the alleged abusers and cut off all contact with them.

Many believed her and with devastating results, including family breakups.

Followers shared several screenshots of those so-called psychic confirmations with W5.

Shanti suggests W5 reporter may have been sexually abused

As an example of how quickly and cavalierly Shanti makes suggestions of past childhood sexual abuse, after the W5 documentary aired, Shanti took to Instagram to write about W5 correspondent and managing editor, Avery Haines.

Shanti wrote that one of the motives for W5 investigating the alleged cult may be that Avery “has deeply repressed CSA (childhood sexual abuse} from around age 4 and is doing this to reaffirm her own denial.”

In August, a Hawaii-jury found that Liana Shanti, aka Liane Wilson, defamed three Canadians from Saskatchewan for calling them Satanists, child abusers and pedophile supporters. The jury awarded the trio C$56 million. That money has not been paid out and Shanti says she plans to appeal.

Shanti has publicly stated that she will litigate her “facts” about the Canadians, and other former followers online. She has continued to post allegations similar to what the jury found to be defamatory.
